items.title: Wittgenstein's later work treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless

Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar and logic, not reducible to scientific or empirical assertion. It is meaningful within its practice, regardless of whether it asserts external facts
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory. 'The meaning of a word is its use in the language.'

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D.Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this 'reduces' religious claims to non-cognitive expressions — but Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: The 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein's move opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.
